Job 1: Protect

The first job is to keep the product in the condition you made it. That means keeping out air, moisture, dust, light, ants and other pests, and surviving the journey from your kitchen to the buyer. In Nigeria that journey can include a hot bus, a dusty market table, a dispatch rider's box in the rain and a shop with no air conditioning. A beautiful label on a pouch that lets air in will still give the buyer soft, stale chin chin. **If the package fails to protect, nothing else matters.**
Job 2: Inform

The second job is to tell the buyer the facts: what the product is, how much is inside, what it is made from, who made it, when it was made, when it should be used by, and how to store and use it. For food, drinks and cosmetics in Nigeria, NAFDAC sets out what a label must carry, and you will study those basics in Module 3. Good information also protects you: when a customer complains, your batch number and dates let you trace exactly which production run she bought.
Job 3: Sell

The third job is to attract the right buyer and help her choose your product over the one beside it. This is where your brand name, logo, colours, photos and short promise come in. Buyers often decide in a few seconds, so the front of your pack must say clearly what the product is and why it is worth the price.

Big companies spend a lot on branding, but the parts are simple and a small business can do them well. A **brand identity** is the set of things that make your product recognisable every time: the name, logo, colours, fonts, the tone of your words and a short promise. When these stay the same on your pouch, your WhatsApp status and your carton, people start to recognise you without reading.

The name

Your brand name should be easy to say, easy to spell when someone searches on WhatsApp or Instagram, and not already used by another business in your product area. Say it aloud in English and in the languages your customers speak, to make sure it does not mean something unfortunate. If you plan to register a business name, you can search for availability on the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) portal before you print anything.

Logo, colours and fonts

A good small-business logo is simple. It should still be readable when printed only 2 cm wide on a small jar, and it should work in a single colour, for example when photocopied or stamped. Many strong logos are just the brand name in a well-chosen font, called a **wordmark**. Fancy drawings with thin lines often disappear when printed small.

Pick a palette of two or three colours: one main colour, one supporting colour, and a neutral such as white, cream or black for text. Record each colour's code (for example a HEX code like #2E7D32) so your printer and designer use exactly the same shade every time. For text, use at most two fonts: one with character for the brand name and one plain, easy-to-read font for information. Dark text on a light background is easiest to read.

**Glass:** excellent barrier, does not react with most products, looks premium, can be reused. It is heavy and breaks, so it needs dividers in cartons. Good for honey, oils, sauces and pepper paste.

**Laminated pouches:** multi-layer film pouches (often with foil or metallised layers) give a strong barrier against air and moisture at a low weight. Good for snacks, spices and powders, sealed with a heat sealer.
**Kraft paper and cardboard:** good for secondary packaging, dry goods and gift boxes, but paper alone does not block moisture or oil. Pair it with a lined inner pouch.
**Metal tins:** strong and light-proof, good for dry goods and balms, but cost more in small quantities.

Food-contact and hygiene rules
Buy new, food-grade containers from a supplier who can tell you the material. Never reuse bottles that held chemicals, fuel, insecticide or detergent for food or cosmetics.
Wash reusable glass jars in hot soapy water, rinse, and dry fully. Many producers then sterilise jars in boiling water or a hot oven before filling.
Pack in a clean, covered area away from animals, with hair covered and hands washed. Keep packed and unpacked items apart.
Fill to the same level each time and wipe the rim before closing, so the seal grips and no product sits under the lid.
Store empty containers covered, off the floor, away from sun and dust.
Heat sealers and hot filling

Impulse heat sealers and hot fills can burn. Keep fingers away from the sealing bar, unplug the sealer when not in use and never leave it on near children. Do not use a sealer with a damaged cable or plug, and do not overload a single extension socket. Let glass jars cool gradually: pouring very hot product into a cold jar, or putting a hot jar on a cold wet surface, can crack it.

Many first labels fail for simple reasons: the label is too long and overlaps badly, text is cut off at the edge, the writing is too small to read, or the printed colours look dull. All of these can be avoided by measuring carefully and setting up the design correctly before you add any decoration. You can do the whole job on a smartphone with the free version of Canva, though a laptop makes fine adjustments easier.

Step 1: Measure the container

For a round jar or bottle, measure the **diameter** (straight across the top or body) and the **height of the flat, straight part** where the label will sit. Avoid the curved shoulder and the base. The distance around a round container is its circumference: **diameter × 3.14**. For a wrap-around label, add a few millimetres of overlap so the ends meet neatly. For a front-only label, measure the flat face you want to cover and leave a small margin on every side.
Worked example: sizing a wrap label for a groundnut butter jar
For example, Bisi in Ibadan packs groundnut butter in round PET jars. The body is 70 mm across and the straight part is 70 mm tall.
Circumference: 70 mm × 3.14 = about 220 mm.
Add 5 mm overlap: label length = 225 mm.
Leave 5 mm clear at top and bottom of the straight part: label height = 70 − 10 = 60 mm.
Add 3 mm bleed on every side for the design file: canvas = 231 mm × 66 mm.
Keep all text at least 3 mm inside the cut line (the safe zone), and keep the overlap area free of important words.
Bisi's printer cuts labels at 225 mm × 60 mm. Because the background extends into the bleed and text stays inside the safe zone, no white edges show and no words are lost.
Step 2: Set up the design in Canva
Open Canva, choose Create a design, then Custom size. Change the unit to millimetres (mm) and type your label size, for example 225 × 60 mm.
Turn on the print bleed guide (in the File menu, look for the option to show print bleed). A dotted line appears near the edge: stretch your background colour right to the outer edge past this line.
Turn on rulers and guides and drag guides 3 mm inside the cut line on each side. This is your safe zone.
Apply your brand kit colours using the HEX codes you saved, and your two chosen fonts.
Step 3: Lay out by order of importance

Designers call this **hierarchy**: the most important thing is biggest and most visible, and the rest follows. On the front panel, a buyer should see, in this order: the **brand name**, the **product name** (what it is), one short **key point** such as "No added sugar" (only if true), and the **net content** such as 250 g. On the back or side, put the information panel: ingredients, directions and storage, manufacturer's name and address, phone, batch number, dates and barcode if you have one.

To find the share of a shared item, divide its cost by the number of units it holds. A carton that costs 600 naira and holds 24 jars adds 25 naira per jar. For wastage, add a percentage based on your own records; if you do not have records yet, start with about 5% and adjust once you have data.
Worked example: full cost and price for 250 g groundnut butter
For example, Bisi works out the cost of one jar. All naira figures are approximate examples; use your own supplier quotes.
Packaging: PET jar with lid 220, label 60, foil seal 15, carton share 25 = 320 naira.
Wastage allowance 5%: 320 × 1.05 = 336 naira.
Product inside (groundnuts, oil, salt, gas): 750 naira. Labour: 150 naira. Share of overheads (transport, phone data, rent): 100 naira.
Full cost per jar: 336 + 750 + 150 + 100 = 1,336 naira.
Wholesale price for a 30% margin on the selling price: 1,336 ÷ 0.70 = about 1,909, rounded to 1,900 naira.
Suggested retail price leaving the shop about 25% of its selling price: 1,900 ÷ 0.75 = about 2,533, rounded to 2,500 naira.

Bisi knows packaging is about a quarter of her full cost, she sells to shops at 1,900 naira and recommends 2,500 naira on the shelf. She checks similar products in two supermarkets to confirm 2,500 naira is realistic.
Margin is not the same as markup

Margin is profit as a share of the selling price. Markup is profit as a share of the cost. Adding 30% to a cost of 1,000 naira gives 1,300 naira, but the margin is only 300 ÷ 1,300, about 23%. To get a true 30% margin, divide the cost by 0.70.
Small runs or large runs?

Printers usually charge much less per label for large orders, because setting up the job costs the same whether they print 100 or 5,000. Packaging suppliers also have a **minimum order quantity (MOQ)**, the smallest amount they will sell. But a large order ties up cash, and if you change your design or your NAFDAC details, unused labels become waste.

Trust is your most valuable brand asset. A customer who feels misled by a label rarely comes back, and she tells others. Honest packaging is both the right thing and the safe thing.

Claims: what you can and cannot say

A **claim** is any statement that promises a quality or benefit, such as "natural", "sugar-free" or "good for skin". Every claim on your package must be true and something you could prove if asked. Medical claims, such as saying a food or cream cures, treats or prevents a disease, are especially risky: on NAFDAC-regulated products these need approval, and making them without it can lead to refusal of registration or enforcement action.

Honest claim

Honest claims describe what is really in the product and how it is made, which you can prove.
**"Organic"** should only be used if you hold a recognised organic certification.
**"Natural"** is vague. Better to name the actual ingredients.
**"Chemical-free"** is never true: water and salt are chemicals. Say what is not added instead, if that is true, for example "no artificial colour".
**"Sugar-free" or "No added sugar"** must match your recipe exactly, every batch.
**Pictures** count as claims too. Do not show fruit that is not in the product.
Worked example: rewriting claims for a shea butter jar
For example, Hauwa's first label says: "Pure organic shea butter. Cures eczema and stretch marks. Chemical-free. Best in Africa."
"Organic": she has no certificate, so she removes it.
"Cures eczema and stretch marks": a medical claim with no approval. She removes it completely.
"Chemical-free": not accurate. She replaces it with "No added fragrance", which is true for this product.
"Best in Africa": cannot be proven. She replaces it with "Hand-whipped in Kaduna from unrefined shea butter", which is true and specific.
She keeps "Pure" only after confirming the jar contains shea butter alone, and lists "Ingredients: shea butter (Butyrospermum parkii)" on the back.
The new label is shorter, honest and still appealing, and it will not cause problems during NAFDAC review or with an unhappy customer.
Original branding and protecting your own

Copying the colours, layout or name style of a famous product to borrow its reputation is unfair, can mislead buyers and can lead to legal action for trademark infringement or passing off. Create your own look. Once your brand starts to sell, protect it: register your business name with CAC and consider registering your brand name and logo as a trademark with the Trademarks, Patents and Designs Registry under the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment. A registered trademark makes it easier to act against someone who copies you.
Inclusive packaging
Use large, plain fonts and strong contrast so older buyers and people with weaker sight can read.
Put the product type and size in words and a simple picture, which helps buyers who read little English.
Add one short line in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or Pidgin if your buyers use it, while keeping English as the main language.
Choose lids and pouches that people with weak hands can open, such as wide screw lids or tear notches.
Show people in your marketing who look like your real customers.
Greener choices that also save money

Packaging waste is visible in Nigerian gutters and markets, and many buyers notice it. You do not need expensive special materials to do better. Use only as much packaging as protection requires, avoid extra plastic layers that do nothing, and choose materials that people reuse, such as sturdy glass jars or strong tubs. Some producers offer a small discount when customers return clean jars, which also cuts container costs. Paper bags and kraft boxes work well as secondary packaging for dry goods. Keep any green claim specific and true: say "Return this jar for 100 naira off your next one" rather than vague words like "eco-friendly".

For example: "Ruby Zobo gives busy office workers a fresh, chilled zobo with no added sugar, made the same morning in small batches." Keep it on your kit page and use the same idea in your captions and pitch.
Write a container specification

A **specification** (spec) is a short, exact description that lets anyone reorder the same thing. Without it, a new batch of jars may arrive with a slightly different neck size, and your old lids or labels will not fit. Write it once and keep it in your project folder.
Container: for example, 250 ml round PET jar, clear, 70 mm diameter, resin code 1
Closure: 70 mm white PP screw lid with foil induction liner or pressure-sensitive seal
Label: 225 × 60 mm waterproof vinyl, gloss, wrap-around with 5 mm overlap
Carton: 24 units with card dividers
Supplier name, contact, last price paid and date, MOQ and delivery time
Show what changed
Reviewers, buyers and funders are most convinced by a clear before-and-after. Put your two photos side by side at the top of your project, with one line under each explaining what changed and why.

Finally, look at the project as an outsider would. Can someone who has never met you understand what your product is, how it is packed, what it costs, how you tested it and whether the label is compliant? If not, add a one-paragraph summary at the top of the folder. Clear organisation is a sign of a serious business, and it saves you time every time you reorder or apply for an opportunity.

Good packaging only helps if people see it. Many of your buyers will first meet your product as a photo on WhatsApp or Instagram, and shop owners will judge it by how you present it. This lesson shows you how to photograph your package well with a phone, list it properly and pitch it with confidence.

Phone product photography
Use daylight: set a table beside a window with indirect light. Avoid harsh midday sun and the yellow light of indoor bulbs.
Use a plain background: a sheet of white cardboard curved up behind the product, or a clean wooden board for a warmer look.
Clean the product: wipe fingerprints and dust, straighten the label and fill to the right level.
Clean the lens with a soft cloth. Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings to keep the product straight and centred.
Do not use digital zoom. Move the phone closer instead, and tap the screen on the label to focus.
Take three standard shots: front at eye level, a three-quarter angle, and the back label so buyers can read details.

Hold the phone steady or prop it against books. Take several photos of each angle and keep the sharpest. Basic edits in your phone's photo app, such as straightening, cropping and a small brightness increase, are fine, but do not change the colours so much that the real product looks different when it arrives.
WhatsApp Business catalogue

The free WhatsApp Business app lets you create a **catalogue**, a small shop window inside your profile. Each item can have photos, a name, a price, a description and a link. Customers can browse and send you the item in a chat. Use your three photos, the exact product name and size, the price, and a short description with ingredients and storage. Add your catalogue link to your status and share it in groups where selling is allowed.

Worked example: pitching to a neighbourhood supermarket
For example, Bisi takes two jars of groundnut butter and her printed sell sheet to a supermarket in Ibadan. Prices are approximate.

The best before date is six months from production. I can supply 12 jars this week, on sale or return for the first month."
She hands over a sample jar and the sell sheet, and asks: "What would you need to see before you stock it?"
The manager says customers ask about NAFDAC numbers and that the jar needs a barcode for the till.

Structure your 30-second pitch
Greet and introduce yourself and your brand in one sentence.
Say what the product is, the size and one true point that makes it different.
Give the retailer's numbers: your price, the suggested shelf price and what she keeps per unit.
Make a small, low-risk offer, such as one carton or a short sale-or-return trial.
Ask a question that invites honest feedback, then listen and write down the answer.

Retailers hear many pitches. What they remember is a seller who knows her numbers, has a clean, compliant package, respects their time and follows up when she said she would. If you are nervous, practise with a friend playing a busy shop owner who interrupts and asks hard questions about price and registration.
Agree terms in writing

Before leaving goods on sale or return, agree in writing (a WhatsApp message is better than nothing) how many units you left, the price, when you will check stock and when unsold or expired goods come back. Keep copies of every delivery note.

Write your reflection

Your reflection should be short and specific, around 150 to 250 words. Answer four questions: What was the biggest weakness of my original package? What feedback surprised me? What did I change because of it, and what was the result? What would I do differently next time? Name real details, for example "Labels smudged in the cooler, so I switched to vinyl and all ten passed", rather than general statements like "I learned a lot".
Build your 90-day plan

A good plan has a few actions, each with a date, a cost and a way to know it is done. Group them into three 30-day blocks. Base the actions on your own gaps: if you are not registered, registration steps come first; if you are, focus on retail outlets and repeat sales.
A 90-day packaging plan
Days 1 to 30: register and finalise
Days 31 to 60: print and list
Days 61 to 90: pitch and measure
Day 90: review and report
Each 30-day block ends with a check against your targets.
Worked example: Funke's 90-day plan

For example, Funke sells Ruby Zobo to offices and has a tested vinyl label, but no CAC registration, NAFDAC number or barcode yet. Costs are approximate and must be confirmed with each agency or supplier.

Days 1 to 30: register her business name with CAC; read NAFDAC's guidance for small producers and list the documents and facility requirements; improve her production space to meet them. Target: CAC certificate received.

Days 31 to 60: submit her NAFDAC application; apply for GS1 barcodes; keep selling to existing office customers with her compliant label minus the NAFDAC number. Target: application submitted, barcodes received.
Days 61 to 90: list Ruby Zobo in her WhatsApp catalogue; pitch to three cafes and one supermarket with her sell sheet; track weekly sales on her scorecard. Target: 2 new outlets, 70 bottles a week.
Day 90: compare her scorecard with her baseline, update her one-page report, and decide whether to order a larger label run once her NAFDAC number is issued.
Funke's plan is realistic because each step depends on the one before, and she does not print large label runs until her regulatory details are final.

What makes a target useful

A useful target is a number you can count, with a date. "Sell more" cannot be checked; "70 bottles a week by day 90" can. Base targets on your baseline: if you sell 50 units a week now, aiming for 70 in three months is a stretch but possible, while aiming for 500 sets you up for disappointment. Choose no more than four targets so your weekly check stays quick.
Sales target: units per week, based on your baseline
Reach target: number of shops, offices or resellers stocking you
Quality target: damage or return rate kept below a set level
Compliance target: the next registration milestone you control
Beware of registration agents who promise shortcuts

Use official NAFDAC, CAC and GS1 Nigeria channels and pay fees through official payment routes. Be very careful with anyone offering to "arrange" a NAFDAC number quickly for a fee outside the official process; a number obtained that way can be invalid and put your business at risk.

Put your plan where you will see it: printed on your wall, or as reminders in your phone calendar for each 30-day check. At each check, update your scorecard, tick off finished actions and adjust the next block. After 90 days, you will have a stronger brand, a compliant package and evidence of what works, which you can use to apply for loans, grants, trade fairs or larger retail contracts.
